question: Can an employer take a tip credit for directly supporting work that exceeds 20% of the tip‑credit workweek?
answer: No, the employer cannot take a tip credit for any time spent on directly supporting work that exceeds the 20 percent tolerance.
quote: The employer cannot take a tip credit for any time spent on directly supporting work that exceeds the 20 percent tolerance.
notes: Scoped to federal contractors: the general FLSA 80/20 dual-jobs rule (531.56(f)) was vacated in 2024, so an unscoped question has a different answer.
revised_question: Under the federal contractor minimum wage rules (Executive Order 13658), can an employer take a tip credit for directly supporting work that exceeds 20 percent of the workweek?
revised_answer: No. It cannot take a tip credit for directly supporting work beyond the 20 percent tolerance (20 percent of the hours for which it takes a tip credit).

question: How long can a tipped employee perform directly supporting work continuously before the employer loses the tip credit for the excess time?
answer: If the continuous period exceeds 30 minutes, the employer cannot take a tip credit for any time beyond 30 minutes.
quote: If a tipped employee performs directly supporting work for a continuous period of time that exceeds 30 minutes, the employer cannot take a tip credit for any time that exceeds 30 minutes.
notes: Scoped to federal contractors: the general FLSA 80/20 dual-jobs rule (531.56(f)) was vacated in 2024, so an unscoped question has a different answer.
revised_question: Under the federal contractor minimum wage rules, how long can a tipped employee do directly supporting work in one continuous stretch before the employer loses the tip credit?
revised_answer: 30 minutes. No tip credit may be taken for any continuous directly supporting work beyond 30 minutes.

question: May an employer take a tip credit for time a tipped employee spends on work that is not part of the tipped occupation?
answer: No, the employer may not take a tip credit for that time.
quote: If a tipped employee is required to perform work that is not part of the employee's tipped occupation, the employer may not take a tip credit for that time.
notes: No number or condition; overlaps c001/c002.

question: Who can file a complaint under this regulation?
answer: Any employee, contractor, labor organization, trade organization, contracting agency, or other person or entity may file a complaint.
quote: Any employee, contractor, labor organization, trade organization, contracting agency, or other person or entity that believes a violation of the Executive Order or this part has occurred may file a complaint with any office of the Wage and Hour Division.

question: Can a complaint be filed in a language other than English?
answer: Yes, the Wage and Hour Division will accept the complaint in any language.
quote: If the complainant is unable to file the complaint in English, the Wage and Hour Division will accept the complaint in any language.
notes: Added context (federal contractor paid sick leave, Part 13).
revised_question: Can a worker on a federal contract file a paid sick leave complaint with the Wage and Hour Division in a language other than English?

question: Will the identity of a complainant be disclosed without their consent?
answer: No, the identity shall not be disclosed without the prior consent of the individual.
quote: the identity of any individual who makes a written or oral statement as a complaint ... shall not be disclosed in any manner to anyone other than Federal officials without the prior consent of the individual.

revised_question: If I complain to the Wage and Hour Division about my federal contractor's paid sick leave, will my identity be revealed?
revised_answer: No. Your identity will not be disclosed to anyone other than Federal officials without your prior consent.

question: Who makes the final determination on whether a citation is issued after an inspection when the Area Director initially finds no citation warranted?
answer: The Assistant Regional Director makes the final determination, and it is not subject to further review.
quote: The determination of the Assistant Regional Director shall be final and not subject to review.

question: Does the issuance of a citation automatically mean a violation of the Act has occurred?
answer: No, a citation does not constitute a finding of a violation unless the citation is not contested or, if contested, is affirmed by the Review Commission.
quote: Every citation shall state that the issuance of a citation does not constitute a finding that a violation of the Act has occurred unless there is a failure to contest as provided for in the Act or, if contested, unless the citation is affirmed by the Review Commission.

question: When can an employer be cited for an employee's rescue activity?
answer: An employer can be cited only if the employee was designated or assigned, or directed as part of job duties, to perform rescue work and the employer failed to provide safety protection, training, and rescue equipment.
quote: No citation may be issued to an employer because of a rescue activity undertaken by an employee of that employer with respect to an individual in imminent danger unless: (1)(i) Such employee is designated or assigned by the employer to have responsibility to perform or assist in rescue operations, and (ii) The employer fails to provide protection of the safety and health of such employee, including failing to provide appropriate training and rescue equipment; or (2)(i) Such employee is directed by the employer to perform rescue activities in the course of carrying out the employee's job duties, and (ii) The employer fails to provide protection of the safety and health of such employee, including failing to provide appropriate training and rescue equipment;
notes: Source passage is cut off mid-list ('; or'), so the 'only if' answer may be incomplete.

question: If I don’t learn right away that a fatality was work‑related, how long do I have to report it to OSHA?
answer: You must report the fatality within eight (8) hours after you learn it was work‑related.
quote: Eight (8) hours for a fatality, and twenty-four (24) hours for an in-patient hospitalization, an amputation, or a loss of an eye.

question: If I learn later that an in‑patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye was work‑related, how quickly must I report it to OSHA?
answer: You must report it within twenty‑four (24) hours after you learn it was work‑related.
quote: Eight (8) hours for a fatality, and twenty-four (24) hours for an in-patient hospitalization, an amputation, or a loss of an eye.
notes: Same sentence as c010; merged into c010.

question: Do I have to report an in‑patient hospitalization that was only for observation or diagnostic testing?

question: Does an applicant for a job count as an employee for protection under section 11(c)?

revised_answer: Not ordinarily; employees of a State or political subdivision are not ordinarily within section 11(c) coverage.

question: Does the Act require covered employees to be paid overtime at premium rates?
answer: No, the Act does not provide for compensation of covered employees at premium rates for overtime hours of work.

notes: 'The Act' was ambiguous; named the Service Contract Act.
revised_question: Does the Service Contract Act itself require overtime pay for covered service employees?
revised_answer: No. The SCA does not require premium pay for overtime, although other Federal laws may.

question: When determining overtime pay required by other Federal laws, are fringe benefit payments that are excluded under the Fair Labor Standards Act included in the regular hourly rate?

question: Where are the fringe benefit payments that qualify for exclusion from the regular rate described?

question: If a contract’s minimum wage includes a fringe benefit that isn’t expressed as an hourly rate, can the contractor provide a different benefit or cash equivalent instead?
answer: Yes, the contractor may either pay the benefit as stated in the wage determination or may pay another bona fide fringe benefit or an hourly cash equivalent thereof.
quote: Whenever the minimum wage rate prescribed in the contract for a class of laborers or mechanics includes a fringe benefit which is not expressed as an hourly rate, the contractor may either pay the benefit as stated in the wage determination or may pay another bona fide fringe benefit or an hourly cash equivalent thereof.

question: When the Wage and Hour Division takes action, does the contractor have to give each affected worker a written copy of the determination, or can it be posted instead?
answer: The contractor must either furnish a written copy of the determination to each affected worker or post it as part of the wage determination.
quote: The contractor must furnish a written copy of such determination to each affected worker or it must be posted as a part of the wage determination.

question: What is required of a contractor if they fail to pay all or part of the wages required by the contract?
answer: The contractor will be required to pay interest on any underpayment of wages.
quote: In the event of a failure to pay all or part of the wages required by the contract, the contractor will be required to pay interest on any underpayment of wages.
notes: Made it a yes/no question and named the contract type.
revised_question: On a Davis-Bacon contract, does a contractor that underpays wages have to pay interest on the underpayment?
revised_answer: Yes. A contractor that fails to pay all or part of the required wages must pay interest on any underpayment.

question: How must an employer mark the payroll records to show which employees earn wages partly from tips?
answer: The employer must place a symbol, letter or other notation on the pay records identifying each employee whose wage is determined in part by tips.
quote: A symbol, letter or other notation placed on the pay records identifying each employee whose wage is determined in part by tips.

question: When the tip credit amount per hour changes, how often must the employer inform the employee in writing?
answer: The employer must report the new tip‑credit amount in writing each time it changes from the amount taken in the preceding week.
quote: The amount per hour which the employer takes as a tip credit shall be reported to the employee in writing each time it is changed from the amount per hour taken in the preceding week.

question: If an employer runs a mandatory tip‑pooling arrangement for employees who receive tips but for whom no tip credit is taken, what record‑keeping step is required regarding employee identification?
answer: The employer must place a symbol, letter, or other notation on the pay records identifying each employee who receives tips.
quote: A symbol, letter, or other notation placed on the pay records identifying each employee who receive tips.

question: Can we rely on the interpretations in this subpart as long as they remain effective?
answer: Yes, reliance may be placed on the interpretations as long as they remain effective and are not modified, amended, rescinded, or determined by judicial authority to be incorrect.

question: Am I required to pay an exempt employee their full salary for a week when they take unpaid FMLA leave?
answer: No, an employer is not required to pay the full salary for weeks in which an exempt employee takes unpaid leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act.

question: Do employer contributions to a bona fide thrift or savings plan have to be included in an employee's regular rate of pay?
answer: No, they do not have to be included if the plan meets the requirements set forth in the regulations.
quote: it is not necessary to include any sums paid to or on behalf of such employee, in recognition of services performed by him during a given period, which are paid pursuant to a bona fide thrift or savings plan meeting the requirements set forth herein.

revised_question: Do employer contributions to a bona fide thrift or savings plan count toward an employee's regular rate for overtime?
revised_answer: No, as long as the plan meets the requirements of 29 CFR part 547.

question: Can contributions made for profit‑sharing or other benefit purposes be excluded from the regular rate when they are part of a combined thrift or savings plan?
answer: Yes, they can be excluded if they meet the tests in Part 549 or the Interpretative Bulletin part 778 §§ 778.214 and 778.215.

question: Do domestic service employees who live in the employer's household have to be paid overtime?

question: Can children under 16 work on their parents' farms?

question: According to the 1963 Equal Pay Act, what five adverse effects did Congress say wage differentials based on sex cause?
answer: They depress wages and living standards for employees necessary for their health and efficiency; prevent the maximum utilization of the available labor resources; tend to cause labor disputes, thereby burdening, affecting, and obstructing commerce; burden commerce and the free flow of goods in commerce; and constitute an unfair method of competition.

source_title: Pub. L. 88-38, Equal Pay Act of 1963 (77 Stat. 56)

question: Under the 1988 Employee Polygraph Protection Act, what is the maximum civil penalty an employer can be assessed for violating the Act?
answer: An employer may be assessed a civil penalty of not more than $10,000.
quote: Subject to paragraph (2), any employer who violates any provision of this Act may be assessed a civil penalty of not more than $10,000.
source_title: Pub. L. 100-347, Employee Polygraph Protection Act of 1988 (102 Stat. 646)
notes: Good history question: today's maximum is inflation-adjusted and much higher than $10,000.

question: Under the 1988 Employee Polygraph Protection Act, what factors does the Secretary consider when determining the amount of a civil penalty?
answer: The Secretary considers the employer’s previous record of compliance with the Act and the gravity of the violation.
quote: In determining the amount of any penalty under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall take into account the previous record of the person in terms of compliance with this Act and the gravity of the violation.
source_title: Pub. L. 100-347, Employee Polygraph Protection Act of 1988 (102 Stat. 646)

question: Under the 1988 Employee Polygraph Protection Act, how are civil penalties collected?
answer: Civil penalties are collected in the same manner as required by subsections (a) through (e) of section 503 of the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act.
quote: Any civil penalty assessed under this subsection shall be collected in the same manner as is required by subsections (a) through (e) of section 503 of the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act (29 U.S.C. 1853) with respect to civil penalties assessed under subsection (a) of such section.
source_title: Pub. L. 100-347, Employee Polygraph Protection Act of 1988 (102 Stat. 646)

question: Under the 1961 Fair Labor Standards Amendments, what sales volume limits must an independently owned local petroleum wholesale enterprise meet to qualify for the exemption?
answer: The enterprise must have annual gross sales of $1,000,000 or less (excluding excise taxes), at least 75 % of its sales must be made within the state, and no more than 25 % of its sales may be to customers who are bulk distributors for resale.
quote: (10) any employee of an independently owned and controlled local enterprise ... engaged in the wholesale or bulk distribution of petroleum products if (A) the annual gross volume of sales of such enterprise is not more than $1,000,000 exclusive of excise taxes, and (B) more than 75 per centum of such enterprise's annual dollar volume of sales is made within the State in which such enterprise is located, and (C) not more than 25 per centum of the annual dollar volume of sales of such enterprise is to customers who are engaged in the bulk distribution of such products for resale;
source_title: Pub. L. 87-30, Fair Labor Standards Amendments of 1961 (75 Stat. 65)
notes: quote_found=False checked: the answer says 'at least 75%', but the statute says 'more than 75 per centum'. The question is also obscure.

question: Under the 1961 amendments, are drivers or driver’s helpers paid by trip rates exempt if the Secretary determines the payment plan reduces their hours to or below the maximum workweek?
answer: Yes, they are exempt if the Secretary finds that the trip‑rate or similar delivery payment plan has the general purpose and effect of reducing their hours to or below the applicable maximum workweek.
quote: (11) any employee employed as a driver or driver's helper making local deliveries, who is compensated for such employment on the basis of trip rates, or other delivery payment plan, if the Secretary shall find that such plan has the general purpose and effect of reducing hours worked by such employees to, or below, the maximum workweek applicable to them under ^ section 7(a).
source_title: Pub. L. 87-30, Fair Labor Standards Amendments of 1961 (75 Stat. 65)

question: According to the 1961 Fair Labor Standards Amendments, does the exemption cover homeworkers who make wreaths from natural evergreens?
answer: Yes, the exemption expressly includes any homeworker engaged in making wreaths composed principally of natural holly, pine, cedar, or other evergreens, including harvesting those materials.
quote: or to any homeworker engaged in the making of wreaths composed principally of natural holly, pine, cedar, or other evergreens (including the harvesting of the evergreens or other forest products used in making such wreaths)
source_title: Pub. L. 87-30, Fair Labor Standards Amendments of 1961 (75 Stat. 65)
